chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Early Global Crises (1929 to 1982)

lessons.title: The Great Depression: When the Banking System Collapsed

body.text: The 1929 stock market crash did not turn a recession into the Great Depression. Collapsing banks did, while the central bank that could have stopped them stood aside.

children.text: On 11 December 1930, New York regulators shut the Bank of United States. It had 57 branches, about $220 million in deposits and 440,000 accounts, most of them belonging to small traders and immigrant families. More than three quarters of those accounts held less than $400. It was the largest bank failure in American history up to that point, and it was only the beginning.

The stock market side of 1929 is a story of its own. This lesson follows the money that sat in banks, because that is where the Depression did its real damage, and where the modern rulebook for fighting crises was written.

children.text: Wave After Wave: The Banking Panics

body.title: How the banking system came apart

events.title: The stock market crashes
events.description: Banks that had lent against shares, and depositors who had lost money in the market, both come under strain.

events.title: The first banking panic
events.description: Caldwell and Company, a Nashville financial group, collapses. Runs spread to its affiliated banks and across the US South and Midwest.

events.title: Bank of United States closes
events.description: The largest US bank failure to date freezes $220 million of deposits in 440,000 accounts in New York.

events.title: The crisis goes international
events.description: Creditanstalt, Austria's largest bank, announces it has lost more than half its capital. Banking stress spreads through Central Europe.

events.title: German banks fail
events.description: Danat-Bank, one of Germany's biggest banks, collapses on 13 July. Germany's banking crisis becomes far larger than Austria's.

events.title: Britain leaves the gold standard
events.description: Investors fear the US will follow and start converting dollars into gold. The pressure lands on American banks.

events.title: The Fed raises rates in the middle of a panic
events.description: To stop gold leaving the country, the Federal Reserve raises interest rates by 2 percentage points, squeezing banks that were already failing.

events.title: The final wave
events.description: Runs become so severe that states begin declaring their own bank holidays, closing banks to stop the withdrawals. Michigan does so on 14 February.

events.title: National bank holiday
events.description: On his third day in office, President Franklin Roosevelt closes every bank in the country.

events.title: Emergency Banking Act
events.description: Congress lets officials inspect banks, reopen only sound ones, inject government capital, and expand the supply of currency.

events.title: Federal deposit insurance begins
events.description: Deposits are insured up to $2,500. Bank runs, which had been routine, almost disappear.

children.text: Why Failing Banks Made Everything Worse

For decades, bank failures were seen as a symptom of the Depression. Ben Bernanke's research in the early 1980s showed they were a cause. In 2022, that work earned him a share of the Nobel Prize in economics, alongside Douglas Diamond and Philip Dybvig. Bank failures deepened the Depression through three channels.

body.caption: Three channels from failed banks to a failed economy

cells: Most money is bank deposits. When a bank failed, its deposits were frozen or lost, and survivors hoarded cash instead of lending
The US money stock fell by a third between 1929 and 1933, so spending collapsed
A failed bank took with it years of knowledge about which local farmers and firms were reliable borrowers
Even creditworthy borrowers could not get loans, so businesses shut
Falling prices meant falling incomes, but debts stayed fixed in money terms
Borrowers defaulted, which caused more bank failures, which pushed prices down further

children.text: The third channel was named by economist Irving Fisher in 1933. It is the most dangerous, because it feeds on itself. When prices fall, the real weight of a fixed debt rises.

body.latex: \text{Real debt burden} = \frac{\text{Debt in money terms}}{\text{Price level}}
body.caption: If prices fall and the debt stays fixed, the real burden rises.

children.text: How the Depression Reached India

India was a British colony, and the rupee was linked to sterling at 1 shilling 6 pence. India had no central bank of its own to cushion the shock. Its economy was mostly agricultural, so the Depression arrived through crop prices, and it hit the people with the least protection.

Wheat prices fell by almost half and raw jute by more than 60%. But land revenue owed to the government and loans owed to the village moneylender were fixed in rupees. This was Irving Fisher's debt deflation, playing out in Indian villages.

body.title: Debt Deflation in a Punjab Village
body.prompt: A cultivator owes a fixed ₹1,000 to a moneylender. Suppose his crop's price moves exactly with the agricultural price index, from 203 in 1929 to 127 in 1931. By roughly what percentage has the amount of crop he must sell to repay the ₹1,000 increased? Round to the nearest whole number.
body.explanation: The crop needed rises in proportion to 203 ÷ 127 = 1.598. So he must sell about 59.8%, or roughly 60%, more crop to repay exactly the same ₹1,000. His debt did not grow by a single rupee, but its real weight grew by more than half.

children.text: To survive, many families sold the one asset they had: gold. Because the rupee price of gold in India was below world prices, exporting it was profitable, and India became a major supplier of gold to the world.

body.label: A Central Bank Born After the Crisis
body.context: The Hilton Young Commission had recommended a central bank for India back in 1926. The Reserve Bank of India Act was passed in 1934, and the RBI opened in Calcutta, moving its central office to Bombay in 1937.

children.text: What the Fed Got Wrong

The rulebook for stopping bank runs already existed. In 1873, British writer Walter Bagehot argued in his book Lombard Street that during a panic, a central bank should lend freely to sound banks, against good collateral, at a high rate. The Fed in the early 1930s largely did not.

body.title: What a lender of last resort should do vs what the Fed did, 1930 to 1933

columns.label: Bagehot's rule
points: Lend freely to banks facing runs
Flood the system with cash until the panic stops

columns.label: The Fed, 1930 to 1933
points: Let thousands of banks fail, many of them small banks outside its membership
Held back from large-scale lending during the early panics
Raised interest rates in October 1931 to defend gold
Allowed the money stock to fall by a third

body.title: The October 1931 Decision
body.question: Why did the Federal Reserve raise interest rates in October 1931, in the middle of a banking crisis?
options: To defend the dollar's link to gold after Britain left the gold standard
To slow down a booming stock market
To punish banks that had lent recklessly
body.explanation: Prices were falling, not rising, so inflation was not the concern. After Britain left gold on 21 September 1931, investors started converting dollars into gold. The Fed raised rates to make holding dollars more attractive and stop the outflow. Under the gold standard, defending the currency came first, even though tighter money pushed more banks into failure.

body.text: History has a sense of irony. Ben Bernanke, the economist who showed how the Fed's inaction deepened the Depression, was chairing the Federal Reserve when Lehman Brothers failed in 2008. This time the Fed lent on a massive scale. Chapter 4 picks up that story.

body.title: Name the Spiral
body.textWithBlank: When falling prices raise the real burden of fixed debts, causing defaults that push prices down further, economists call it debt ___.
body.explanation: Debt deflation, the term Irving Fisher used in 1933. It is one of the main reasons central banks today treat falling prices as a serious danger, not good news.

children.text: The Fix That Still Protects You

The Roosevelt administration's response worked because it rebuilt confidence, not just banks. The national bank holiday stopped the runs. The Emergency Banking Act let only inspected, sound banks reopen, which told depositors those banks were safe. Federal deposit insurance from 1934 removed the reason to run at all: if the government guarantees your deposit, there is no need to be first in the queue.

body.caption: The 1930s idea, still at work in India today

cells: Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC), an RBI subsidiary
Stop runs by removing the fear of losing deposits

body.title: Save the Small-Town Bank
body.scenario: It is 1932. A small bank in a farming town in Iowa has sound loans, but falling crop prices have made farmers slow to repay. After a bank in the next town fails, depositors start queueing to withdraw. The bank has enough cash for about three days of withdrawals at this pace. There is no deposit insurance.
body.prompt: Using what you learnt in this lesson and in Chapter 1, explain what will probably happen without help, and what two policies would most likely have saved this bank.
body.modelAnswer: Without help, the run will drain the bank's cash in about three days. It will then be forced to sell or call in farm loans in a hurry, at a large discount, turning an illiquid but sound bank into an insolvent one, exactly the fire sale mechanism from Chapter 1. Its depositors lose money, local farmers lose their source of credit, and the failure frightens depositors in the next town, spreading the run. Two policies would most likely have saved it. First, a lender of last resort following Bagehot's rule: the central bank lends the bank cash against its good farm loans, so it can pay every depositor who asks and the run burns out. Second, deposit insurance: if depositors know their money is guaranteed, most never join the queue in the first place. The US got both tools only in 1933 and 1934, too late for about 9,000 banks.

body.title: Go deeper: why the gold standard tied the Fed's hands

children.text: Under the gold standard, every dollar was convertible into a fixed amount of gold, and the Fed had to hold gold reserves to back the currency. That created a hard limit.
To stop bank runs, the Fed needed to create more money and lend it to banks.
Creating more money raised fears that dollars would be worth less gold in future.
Those fears pushed foreigners and depositors to swap dollars for gold, draining reserves.
To protect its gold, the Fed kept money tight or even raised rates, as in October 1931.

Countries that left the gold standard earlier, like Britain in 1931, were free to ease money and generally began recovering sooner. The US effectively left in 1933. The lesson for later crises is that a fixed exchange rate can force a central bank to choose between defending the currency and saving the banks. You will see that same trap in Thailand in 1997.

points: About 9,000 US banks suspended operations between 1930 and 1933, and the money stock fell by a third
Bank failures deepened the Depression by destroying money, cutting off credit, and feeding debt deflation
The Fed failed as a lender of last resort and even raised rates in October 1931 to defend gold
India felt the Depression through collapsing crop prices, fixed debts and large distress gold exports, and got its own central bank, the RBI, only in 1935
The fixes that finally worked, a bank holiday, inspected reopening and deposit insurance, are the ancestors of the DICGC cover that protects Indian depositors today
